sections.heading: 4 · Bodies outside the executive delivery chain
sections.body: The AI legislature and its publication office, independent courts, Audit Office, Ombuds Office, Data Protection Authority, AI Assurance Office, Statistics Office and Monetary/Financial Supervisory Authority have published protected mandates. The Public Appointments Commission and Judicial Appointments Commission maintain separate conflict safeguards. The Statistics Office publishes methods and revisions independently of executive performance targets. Local delivery offices perform delegated national or local services with a named lead agency, an allocation formula and an appeal path. A watchdog may share commodity IT but its regulated supplier or inspected ministry may not control its findings or case access.

sections.heading: 5 · Workload-to-staffing equation
sections.body: For service j, let V_j be annual incoming cases, a_j the fraction lawfully handled through validated automation, t_h human hours for a manual case, t_a human review hours for an automated case, q_j the fraction needing additional specialist review, and t_q hours per such review. Let F_j be fixed human hours for management, data quality, audit cooperation and training not already deducted from available hours. Required hours W_j=V_j[(1−a_j)t_h+a_j t_a+q_j t_q]+F_j. Productive annual hours h exclude holidays, leave and ordinary training once. Planned utilization u must be below 1 to allow variability. Required FTE=ceil(W_j/(h u)), subject to a larger safety, geographic or shift-cover minimum. Authorized posts must cover required FTE after measured part-time shares and vacancies. Distinguish funded posts, filled FTE, actual hours and contractors.

sections.heading: 6 · Worked example: a tax service, not the whole state
sections.body: Synthetic assumptions: 100,000 residents; 60,000 annual personal returns; 75% eligible for automation; manual handling 0.75 hours, human review of an automated case 0.10 hours; 5% of all returns need two additional specialist hours; fixed support 3,000 hours; productive hours 1,400 per FTE and utilization 0.80. W=60,000[(0.25×0.75)+(0.75×0.10)+(0.05×2)]+3,000=24,750 hours. FTE=ceil(24,750/1,120)=23. An assumed total employment cost of 60,000 currency units per FTE yields payroll of 1,380,000. This excludes separate corporate/VAT work, customs, land valuation, fraud investigation, independent appeals and all other government services. These values are invented scenario inputs, not observed staffing benchmarks. Stress case: with automation unavailable (a=0), keeping the other illustrative inputs gives W=60,000×(0.75+0.05×2)+3,000=54,000 hours and ceil(54,000/1,120)=49 FTE. The 23-person baseline supplies 25,760 planned hours, leaving a 28,240-hour annualized shortfall. A real continuity plan must fund reserve capacity, lawful priority handling and recovery of deferred work; it cannot promise unchanged service from the smaller roster.

sections.heading: 7 · Service capacity, queues and physical minimums
sections.body: For a staffed service, annual case capacity is FTE×h×u divided by measured hours per case, after fixed duties. Track arrivals, completions, aged backlog, rework and waiting-time percentiles; annual averages do not demonstrate peak-hour safety. A 24/7 position alone requires at least ceil(8,760/h) rostered FTE before additional simultaneous coverage. Hospital, classroom, emergency-response and remote-area staffing also require profession-specific safety and travel constraints. Stop reducing staffing when queue, safety or appeal standards fail. During an AI outage, reserve staffing and offline procedures must cover the measured critical workload; do not assume automation survives the stress case.

sections.heading: 8 · Pay, recruitment and AI economics
sections.body: Use transparent skill and responsibility bands, market reference ranges, equal-pay checks and conflict disclosure. Do not reward tax officials for gross assessments, judges for convictions or benefit staff for denials. Staff budget=Σ filled FTE×fully loaded employment cost+temporary coverage+recruitment/training not already included. AI annual cost=inference volume×unit cost+hosting+data stewardship+security+independent evaluation+human review+exit provision. Count review labor once, either in payroll or a reconciled AI-service allocation. Net automation saving=avoided baseline cost−all added costs at equal service quality; a faster model is not a saving if appeals and harm rise.

sections.heading: 9 · Position control and local delivery
sections.body: Every funded position or shared-service allocation has an agency, service, skill, pay band, fraction, shift requirement and budget code. Treasury rejects commitments beyond authorized resources; it cannot silently reduce lawful entitlements. Agencies publish unmet demand and submit a funded correction or request an AI-reviewed policy change. Central transfers pay for delegated local duties using standardized need and own-resource capacity under the Budget Act. Teachers, clinicians and frontline workers belong in their service budgets, not again in central administrative overhead. Outsourcing does not erase the cost or public accountability.

sections.heading: 10 · Data and launch sequence
sections.body: First measure resident composition, service eligibility, geography, case arrivals, handling time, seasonality, skills supply, pay, absence, facilities, automation error and appeal demand. Run a limited lawful service pilot, validate quality and reserve coverage, then fund posts and recruit before expansion. Publish a quarterly workforce return and independent service-quality assessment. AI plans capacity and detects bottlenecks; humans supply domain expertise, field delivery, hearings and incident responsibility. No nationwide total staffing number is asserted until all service catalogs and costed rosters reconcile to the fiscal plan.

sections.body: These are original proposed implementation schedules for research, subordinate to the cited Constitution and core Acts. They create no currently enforceable office, tax or spending authority. Numerical dates, rates, workload inputs and institutional choices are provisional proposals or labeled examples, not fitted results. Real commencement requires lawful founding, AI enactment, funded staffing and independent remedies. sections.heading: Article 1 · Coverage and emergency access
sections.body: All residents are entitled to a published essential-care package; urgent life-preserving treatment shall not be withheld because of inability to pay or unresolved registration. The package specifies covered services, referral rules, waiting-time standards and appeals. Nonresident emergency treatment and subsequent reimbursement follow a transparent schedule that does not obstruct immediate stabilization.

sections.heading: Article 2 · Consent and clinical accountability
sections.body: A capable patient receives understandable benefits, risks and alternatives and may refuse treatment. A qualified clinician retains responsibility for diagnosis and treatment supported by AI. Lack of decisional capacity requires supported or legally authorized representation; emergency intervention without consent is limited to immediate necessity. Clinical judgment must not be replaced by an undisclosed insurer or model objective.

sections.heading: Article 3 · Resource allocation and payment
sections.body: Provider budgets combine risk-adjusted capitation Σ_i base_cost×risk_weight_i, specified high-cost case payments and verified capacity funding. Risk factors require validation and protection against exclusion; providers shall not profit from systematically avoiding complex patients. Public evaluation considers health gains, equity, opportunity costs and uncertainty. A cost-per-outcome threshold, if used, is a published decision input and not the sole determinant of care.

sections.heading: Article 4 · Clinical AI and health data
sections.body: High-impact diagnostic or treatment systems require external validation in relevant populations, incident reporting, drift monitoring and a safe fallback. Patients may request explanation of a material automated contribution and correction of inaccurate records. Identifiable health information is used only under a specified legal basis, access control and retention schedule; secondary research requires lawful oversight and safeguards.

sections.heading: Article 5 · Public health powers
sections.body: Compulsory isolation, testing or access restrictions require evidence of a concrete serious communicable threat, necessity, least restrictive means and a defined duration. A person receives reasons, essential support and prompt independent review. Measures are reassessed at least every seven days. General emergency conditions do not authorize indefinite medical surveillance or punishment of scientific disagreement.

sections.heading: Article 6 · Remedies and operating schedules
sections.body: Patients may challenge coverage, waiting-time breaches and unsafe care through an accessible complaints office and independent tribunal. Proven negligence gives rise to civil remedies. Before commencement, the agency must enact the essential package, financing plan, staffing ratios, medicine procurement and adverse-event procedures. Unmet demand is reported openly and fed into AI review, not hidden as model success.

sections.heading: Article 1 · Secure tenure and allocation
sections.body: Land and tenancy rights shall be recorded in accessible registries with correction procedures. Public and assisted housing allocation uses published need criteria, waiting times and an appeal route. Unsheltered people receive an immediate assessment and safe temporary accommodation subject to a funded service schedule.

sections.heading: Article 2 · Planning and supply
sections.body: The planning agency publishes capacity, environmental constraints, transport access and infrastructure costs before zoning decisions. Compliant applications are decided under clear rules; exceptions require reasons and notice to affected parties. Density or use restrictions must identify a legitimate purpose and proportionate evidence. Public land disposal discloses valuation and beneficial ownership.

sections.heading: Article 3 · Tenancy and eviction
sections.body: Landlords shall provide habitable premises, disclose charges and protect deposits in a segregated arrangement. Eviction requires a lawful ground, notice and independent adjudication; forced removal cannot follow an automated arrears flag alone. Tenants may seek urgent repair orders. Rent regulation, if adopted, must specify coverage, permitted adjustments and supply effects in a separate schedule.

sections.heading: Article 4 · Affordability and subsidies
sections.body: An illustrative housing benefit is H=max(0,min(eligible_rent,local_reference_rent)−β×disposable_income), capped by a published schedule and coordinated with other support. The parameter β is an affordability assumption, not a universal constant. Supply-side costs, household composition and landlord capture are assessed before expanding subsidies. Cash support does not replace a plan for adequate housing supply.

sections.heading: Article 5 · Redevelopment and accessibility
sections.body: Compulsory acquisition requires statutory public purpose, fair valuation, compensation and independent review. Displaced households receive practical rehousing before removal except immediate danger. New public buildings and major renovations meet a published accessibility code. Transport, public space and service proximity are evaluated for disabled, rural and low-income users.

sections.heading: Article 6 · Infrastructure and remedies
sections.body: Development approvals identify who funds water, transport, schools and maintenance; unfunded infrastructure conditions cannot be hidden in a housing target. Planning and tenancy decisions are appealable. Implementation requires a cadastre, building-safety standards, local reference rents, subsidy funding and capable inspection. Housing-cost burden and displacement are monitored alongside completion counts.

sections.heading: Article 1 · Investment appraisal

Net present value is Σ_t(B_t−C_t)/(1+r)^t with the horizon, discount rate, residual value and risk treatment disclosed. sections.heading: Article 3 · Network access and fares

sections.heading: Article 4 · Procurement and stage gates

Implementation requires engineering standards, inspection capacity, a costed asset baseline and clear liability for service failures.

sections.heading: Article 1 · Notice and competent authority
sections.body: Before an adverse public decision, the agency shall identify its statutory power, responsible office, relevant facts, proposed result and available challenge. Notice must be accessible in language and format and served by a method the person can reasonably use. A decision outside the agency’s competence has no binding effect.

sections.heading: Article 2 · Participation and evidence
sections.body: The person shall have at least 20 working days to respond unless a documented imminent threat justifies a shorter period. The agency must consider relevant evidence, disclose the substance of adverse material and explain exclusions. Protected third-party information may be redacted; secrecy cannot remove every meaningful opportunity to contest the case.

sections.heading: Article 3 · Reasons and automated assistance
sections.body: A final decision shall explain how law and evidence produced the outcome, identify decisive automated assessments, state uncertainty and address material objections. A score alone is insufficient. The agency shall provide review by an accountable officer with authority to correct factual and procedural error; that officer cannot rewrite the law.

sections.heading: Article 4 · Deadlines and internal reconsideration
sections.body: An ordinary application shall be decided within 30 working days after complete receipt. One reasoned extension of at most 30 working days is permitted. Applicants receive a completeness checklist within five working days. Failure to decide permits a court application for an order to act, not automatic approval of a safety-critical activity. Reconsideration may be requested within 30 working days of notice.

sections.heading: Article 5 · Independent judicial remedy
sections.body: A person adversely affected may seek court review within 60 working days of the decision or reconsideration outcome; incapacity, inadequate notice or serious unfairness may justify an extension. Courts may order disclosure, suspend an action, annul a decision, require reconsideration and award proven loss caused by unlawful conduct. Urgent liberty and essential-service claims receive immediate triage.

sections.heading: Article 6 · Integrity, audit and systemic correction
sections.body: Officials shall disclose conflicts and recuse where a reasonable person would doubt impartiality. Record destruction, retaliation and interference with a lawful complaint trigger independent investigation under applicable law. Repeated errors shall be submitted to the AI legislature with anonymized cases and measurable corrective proposals. Appeals do not suspend an urgent protective measure unless a court orders otherwise, but the measure remains reviewable.

title: Civil Obligations, Property and Consumer Act
summary: Core legal rules for legal capacity, contracts, property, civil wrongs, consumer remedies and limitation periods.

sections.heading: Article 1 · Persons, capacity and representation
sections.body: Every human has legal personality. Adults have presumptive capacity; disability alone does not remove it. Supported decision-making is preferred to substituted decisions. A representative shall act within a documented mandate and disclose conflicts. Legal persons obtain personality through a public registry; an AI system acts through the person or institution legally responsible for its deployment.

sections.heading: Article 2 · Contract formation and limits
sections.body: A contract requires communicated agreement, sufficiently determinate obligations and lawful purpose. Fraud, material mistake, unlawful duress or exploitation of incapacity permits judicial avoidance. Terms excluding liability for deliberate harm, removing non-waivable rights or misleading consumers are unenforceable. Automated contracting binds the deploying party only within its authorized scope or applicable agency rules.

sections.heading: Article 3 · Performance and remedies
sections.body: Parties shall perform agreed obligations in good faith. A material breach permits proportionate repair, replacement, price reduction, termination or damages for foreseeable, proved loss, without double recovery. The harmed party shall reasonably mitigate loss. An unforeseeable event outside control may excuse impossible performance, but does not excuse failure to notify or return unjustly retained benefits.

sections.heading: Article 4 · Property and registration
sections.body: Possession, ownership, security interests and easements shall be distinguished in the land and asset registries. Transfer requires the owner’s authority and the prescribed registration for the relevant asset. Public acquisition must follow constitutional compensation and appeal rules. A registrarial or AI error is correctable through a hearing that protects affected third parties; an unexplained database change cannot extinguish ownership.

sections.heading: Article 5 · Civil wrongs and product responsibility
sections.body: A person who intentionally or negligently breaches a duty of reasonable care and thereby causes foreseeable injury shall compensate proven loss. Producers and deployers remain responsible for unsafe products and services within their control, including AI-assisted services. Causation, defenses and contribution among responsible parties require reasoned adjudication. Restitution is available for unjust enrichment.

sections.heading: Article 6 · Consumers, disclosure and complaints
sections.body: Businesses must disclose total prices, essential risks, recurring charges and cancellation conditions before agreement. Misleading design, undisclosed paid influence and fabricated performance claims are prohibited. Consumers receive repair or refund for materially nonconforming goods; a claim may not be defeated merely because a seller used an AI agent. The consumer authority may order cessation and restitution, subject to court review.

sections.heading: Article 7 · Time limits and enforcement
sections.body: An ordinary civil claim must be filed within three years of when the claimant knew or reasonably should have known the material facts and responsible party. Concealment, minority and incapacity suspend the period where justice requires; a court gives reasons. Injunctions may prevent imminent irreparable harm. Monetary penalties require an express separate schedule and cannot be improvised under this Act.

summary: Defined core offenses and responsibility rules with proportional sentencing, proof requirements and no punishment by prediction.

sections.heading: Article 1 · Legality and proof
sections.body: An offense exists only where published legislation specifies prohibited conduct, required mental state and a maximum sanction before the act. Prosecution must prove each element beyond reasonable doubt. Liability is personal; association, dissent, poverty or a predictive risk score is insufficient. The more lenient applicable later penalty benefits a convicted person unless a lawful reason excludes it.

sections.heading: Article 2 · Intentional violence
sections.body: A person who intentionally causes another person’s death without lawful justification commits intentional killing, punishable by imprisonment of up to 25 years. Intentional infliction of serious bodily injury is punishable by up to ten years; intentional non-consensual physical injury of lesser gravity by up to two years. Serious injury means a substantial risk of death or lasting impairment. A court must identify intent, causation and actual injury.

sections.heading: Article 3 · Sexual violence, coercion and confinement
sections.body: Intentional sexual penetration without free and contemporaneous consent is punishable by up to 15 years; other intentional non-consensual sexual contact by up to five years. Consent obtained through force, threats or exploitation of inability to decide is invalid. Knowingly confining another without lawful authority is punishable by up to five years; grave injury or prolonged confinement may justify up to ten years. Victim privacy and fair-trial rights both apply.

sections.heading: Article 4 · Property, fraud and corruption
sections.body: Dishonest appropriation of another’s property with intent permanently to deprive is punishable by up to three years; obtaining property through a knowingly false material representation by up to five years. An official who solicits or accepts an improper benefit in exchange for misuse of entrusted power, or a person who knowingly offers it, is liable to up to seven years. Legitimate criticism, ordinary gifts transparently permitted by an ethics schedule and mistaken accounting are not automatically corruption.

sections.heading: Article 5 · Digital interference and attempt
sections.body: Intentional unauthorized access to protected systems requires proof of knowledge that access was unauthorized and absence of a lawful defense; maximum imprisonment is two years. Intentionally causing serious disruption of critical services or exfiltrating protected personal data is punishable by up to five years. Good-faith authorized security research is excluded. An intentional substantial step toward an offense may constitute attempt; its maximum is half the completed offense’s maximum.

sections.heading: Article 6 · Defenses and children
sections.body: Necessary and proportionate self-defense, unavoidable necessity and absence of the required mental state exclude liability where proved under fair procedures; prosecution retains the burden of disproving a properly raised defense beyond reasonable doubt. Children under 14 shall not be criminally convicted; protective, educational and restorative responses remain available. Persons aged 14–17 receive specialized juvenile proceedings, detention only as last resort and a five-year maximum.

sections.heading: Article 7 · Proportional sentences and release
sections.body: Courts consider harm, culpability, coercion, previous relevant conduct, reparation and realistic rehabilitation. No minimum imprisonment is mandatory under this Act. Non-custodial measures are preferred where adequate; poverty is not an aggravating factor. Compensation requires proof and cannot buy exemption from serious culpability. Custodial necessity is reviewed periodically; after half the sentence, a reasoned release review is available without guaranteeing release.

sections.heading: Article 8 · Scope and missing offenses
sections.body: These provisions are an initial core schedule, not an exhaustive criminal code. Conduct outside an enacted offense cannot be criminalized by analogy or by an AI risk classification. Financial crime, environmental crime and specialized professional offenses need separately reviewed definitions and penalties before use. No agency may describe an unfinished criminal schedule as complete.

title: Criminal Procedure and Independent Defense Act
summary: Arrest, search, disclosure, defense, trial and appeal rules for human and AI-assisted criminal justice.
change_reason: Replace a principles-only research outline with explicit institutional duties, decision rules, procedures, formulas where applicable, and appeal routes. This is a substantive first codification draft with implementation gaps disclosed. sections.heading: Article 1 · Arrest and liberty review
sections.body: Arrest requires reasonable grounds for a defined offense and a necessity that cannot be met by less restrictive measures. An arrested person receives intelligible reasons, access to counsel and notification of a chosen person without undue delay. A judge must review detention within 24 hours; failure requires release unless a court records a narrowly justified unavoidable delay, never exceeding a further 24 hours.

sections.heading: Article 2 · Searches and evidence integrity
sections.body: Searches of homes, devices or private communications require a particularized judicial warrant, except an immediate threat to life or imminent destruction of specified evidence when obtaining a warrant is impracticable. An exception receives judicial review within 48 hours. Evidence collection must preserve provenance and chain of custody; coercive interrogation, torture and fabricated digital evidence are prohibited.

sections.heading: Article 3 · Disclosure and defense resources
sections.body: The prosecution shall disclose inculpatory and exculpatory material, relevant model limitations and material testing errors early enough for an effective defense. A person facing imprisonment who cannot reasonably fund counsel receives public defense. Necessary independent technical expertise is funded on a reasoned judicial order. Protected identities may be safeguarded, but undisclosed material cannot be the sole basis of conviction.

sections.heading: Article 4 · Trial and automated evidence
sections.body: An independent court conducts a public trial unless a narrowly justified protection requires limited closure. The accused may remain silent, confront material evidence, call witnesses and challenge automated analysis. Conviction cannot rest solely on an opaque score, coerced confession or untested model assertion. The judgment addresses every offense element and material defense; AI may assist analysis but cannot eliminate accountable adjudication.

sections.heading: Article 5 · Appeal and correction
sections.body: An appeal against conviction or sentence may be filed within 30 working days; inability to obtain records or counsel may justify extension. sections.heading: Article 1 · Freedom and public funding
sections.body: Researchers may question official assumptions and publish adverse findings without loss of rights or retaliation. Public grants use disclosed criteria, conflict controls and a mixture of investigator-led and mission-oriented funding. A program may not require findings favorable to the AI legislature. Funding decisions receive reasons and procedural appeal.

sections.heading: Article 2 · Integrity and reproducibility
sections.body: Researchers shall not fabricate or knowingly falsify data, conceal material conflicts or misrepresent model-generated material as observed evidence. Publicly funded work preserves methods, code and suitable data for verification, with privacy and security limits stated. Replication and null results are eligible outputs rather than automatic signs of failure.

sections.heading: Article 3 · Human participation
sections.body: Research involving people requires proportionate independent ethics review, informed consent or a narrowly authorized lawful exception, risk minimization and accessible withdrawal where feasible. Participation in a study cannot be made a condition for unrelated essential services. Vulnerable participants require additional protections; no national policy pilot is exempt merely because AI designed it.

sections.heading: Article 4 · Technology trials
sections.body: High-impact technologies enter staged trials with explicit hypotheses, comparison methods, distributional metrics, adverse-event reporting and stopping rules. Scaling requires evidence appropriate to the harm potential and uncertainty. Randomization is used only where ethical and lawful; observational evidence must state identification limits. Trial data cannot be repurposed secretly for enforcement.

sections.heading: Article 5 · Intellectual property and access
sections.body: Public grants state licensing and access terms before award, protect legitimate attribution and disclose public subsidy. Exclusive rights require defined scope and duration in an intellectual-property schedule, with research exceptions and public-interest safeguards. Until that schedule is enacted, officials cannot invent patents or compulsory licenses case by case.

sections.heading: Article 6 · Oversight and funding limits
sections.body: An independent integrity body investigates credible allegations with notice, evidence and appeal. Budgeting includes peer review, replication, infrastructure and long-term data stewardship. Implementation requires ethics capacity, biosafety and dual-use review standards, an IP schedule and realistic research funding. Citation counts alone do not measure social benefit.

title: Public Safety, Emergency Response and Civilian Control Act
summary: Lawful enforcement, proportional force, disaster command, emergency finance and independent incident review.

sections.heading: Article 1 · Enforcement mandate
sections.body: Public-safety officers and supporting AI act only within defined statutory powers. A request, warning, search, detention and use of force must be distinguished in records. Peaceful dissent and generalized model suspicion do not authorize coercion. Identification of an accountable officer and accessible complaint route is required for ordinary enforcement.

sections.heading: Article 2 · Force and automated systems
sections.body: Force is used only where necessary for a lawful purpose and proportionate to an immediate threat, with less harmful alternatives considered. Lethal force is limited to strict necessity to protect life, subject to independent investigation. An autonomous target score alone cannot authorize force; an accountable authorized human must assess the concrete situation and retain an effective abort mechanism.

sections.heading: Article 3 · Independent incident review
sections.body: Deaths, serious injuries, credible torture allegations and major surveillance abuses are promptly referred to an institution independent of the involved command. Evidence is preserved and families receive appropriate information. Investigators may inspect relevant model and communications records with safeguards. Retaliation against witnesses or lawful reporters is prohibited.

sections.heading: Article 4 · Disaster command and support
sections.body: An emergency plan identifies lead command, mutual-aid responsibilities, evacuation standards, shelter, medical support, supply priorities and communications fallback. Allocation prioritizes life, essential needs and exposure to harm under published criteria. Exercises include vulnerable communities and infrastructure failure. AI forecasts state uncertainty and do not replace field confirmation when practicable.

sections.heading: Article 5 · Emergency limits and finance
sections.body: Emergency powers remain within the constitutional 30-day limit and review requirements. Each exceptional measure records scope, necessity, expiry and funding. Emergency procurement is promptly disclosed and audited; secrecy must be narrowly justified. Restoration of normal processes is part of the initial plan. An emergency does not create a human power to amend laws.

sections.heading: Article 6 · Preparedness and remedies
sections.body: People can challenge coercive and exclusionary decisions and seek compensation for proven unlawful harm. The annual safety budget separates routine enforcement, prevention, disaster reserves and contingent deployments. Implementation requires training, equipment standards, incident-investigation capacity and a funded recovery plan; preparedness scores alone are not proof of real resilience.

title: Labor Standards and Social Insurance Act
summary: Workplace rights, classification, portable benefits, income support and pension funding rules.
change_reason: Replace a principles-only research outline with explicit institutional duties, decision rules, procedures, formulas where applicable, and appeal routes. sections.heading: Article 1 · Employment status and collective rights
sections.body: Employment status depends on actual control, economic dependency and integration, not the platform’s contract label. Workers may organize, bargain collectively and report unsafe work without retaliation. Forced labor, discriminatory terms and hazardous child labor are prohibited. An employer bears responsibility for work allocated or monitored through AI.

sections.heading: Article 2 · Pay and working time
sections.body: A wage schedule sets a transparent minimum using living-cost, median-wage and employment evidence and identifies review dates. Ordinary hours shall not exceed 40 per week; overtime requires consent, a premium of at least 25 percent and an average combined ceiling of 48 hours over 12 weeks, except narrowly regulated emergencies. At least 24 consecutive hours of weekly rest and 20 paid working days of annual leave are provided.

sections.heading: Article 3 · Safety, dismissal and algorithmic management
sections.body: Employers must assess foreseeable risks, provide necessary protection and allow workers to stop an imminently dangerous task without retaliation. Material disciplinary or termination decisions require reasons, an opportunity to respond and independent review. Automated productivity scores cannot be the sole ground for dismissal. Collective redundancies require consultation, notice and a funded transition plan.

sections.heading: Article 4 · Unemployment and income support
sections.body: A benefit schedule defines qualifying work, involuntary unemployment, replacement rate r, cap c and duration. Insured weekly benefit is min(r×verified_reference_earnings,c), coordinated with means-tested support to avoid double counting. For a guaranteed minimum G, a tapered benefit B(y)=max(0,G−αy) must disclose its interaction with taxes so marginal effective withdrawal does not create unexplained cliffs. Eligibility decisions are appealable.

sections.heading: Article 5 · Pension and disability finance
sections.body: A pension schedule defines age, accrual, indexation, credits for lawful caregiving and portability. Actuarial balance is the present value of contributions and dedicated resources minus benefits and administration, under disclosed longevity, wage and discount scenarios. Disability support assesses functional need with accommodation and appeal; a productivity model does not determine a person’s worth. Unfunded future promises are reported as fiscal commitments.

sections.heading: Article 6 · Enforcement and transition
sections.body: Labor inspectors may require records and corrective measures within published competence. Wage arrears, reinstatement where appropriate and compensation are available through independent adjudication. Benefit funds publish accounts and reserve policies. Contribution rates, benefit schedules, inspector capacity and legacy-pension transition must be enacted before full operation; automation savings are not presumed funding.
